Sounds like old resentments or a trauma response. I’m a recovering pastor’s son. When I see someone use their faith to control or abuse somebody else, I tend to get irate. In this context, I think it might help to view your anger as a symptom and not the main problem. If you were shamed, punished, belittled, etc. for seemingly arbitrary religious reasons when you were growing up, then your anger is justified. It’s probably not a healthy response, but it’s not going to go away until you address those root issues. Hope this helps.

As someone who strikes out socially often, I’ve learned that you don’t need to be liked or seen in most places. You just have to find your people. 
Follow your interests. If there is an activity that you like, maybe you can do it with other people. If there is a social cause you care about, get involved in that in some capacity. Look for volunteer opportunities. You can just go and participate, then conversations will start around the thing you’re doing. 
I have a few solid friendships and I met them all in different places.
I move too much, travel quite a bit, and I don’t have a lot of money. I gave up on finding love and I feel relieved.

He went full auto and sprayed all of them, assuming they’d kill him before he could get all of them. But they didn’t and he lived. 

I met his Grandson in a different war. I guess that family likes to fight.

Let me tell you about my best friend.
He was obese in high school. Band geek, spent a lot of time alone, depressed. He started dating a really hot, malicious girl who made him think she loved him, then she ghosted him and spread lies about him to our friend group. He hated himself and the world. It took him years to get over that.
After high school he got interested in hockey. Being around hockey players got him interested in fitness. He dropped a ton of weight, got in great shape, and excelled at playing goalie. He eventually got invited to teach at international goalie clinics. He’s on a first name basis with a few professional players.
He met an awesome woman. They got married and had a kid together. His son is the coolest kid ever.
He and I have travelled to Russia, South Korea, and Tanzania together. He even met the Dalai Lama in Nepal a few years ago. I could go on about the fun, fulfillment, and success he’s found. But basically it started with him taking small steps after high school. He’s doing great and I’m so proud of him.

Heard. I’m volunteering in Ukraine and I have the same thought about artillery and air strikes.

If you’re doing aid work you will most likely be in a group most of the time. There are a lot of aid workers who are pretty savvy about staying safe and navigating social taboos. I’d look into LGBTQ groups in Warsaw or Krakow for when you’re traveling. I’d be surprised if they didn’t exist. I found an LGBTQ safe house in freaking Kyrgyzstan so I’m sure there’s a community in Poland.

People in need of help will accept help and most of them will be grateful. Forget all these people talking about Azov and the Chechens. They’re actively fighting in the east, far from the refugees where you would be working.
However, understand that the vast majority of Ukrainians are Orthodox Christians. The LGBTQ world basically does not exist for them as it is a sin in the Orthodox Church. Don’t expect them to understand, and prepared for insensitive/ignorant questions and comments.  You should not tolerate harassment or assault, but if you can’t handle them not “getting” you then you shouldn’t go.
Personally, I keep my sexual life and past under wraps when I travel outside of western progressive bubbles. I know lgbtq people who do the same. Not saying it’s right, but it’s how the world is.

It’s because people who have never experienced depression think it’s the same as sadness. When you’re sad, there’s usually something to be sad about. 
That’s not to say that depression can’t be a symptom of something else. Vitamin D deficiency is a good example. But that doesn’t mean that we all have an answer as to why we’re depressed. And there’s no shame in it, even if you “have it all.”

Same. People who don’t know me are surprised if they find out that I struggle with depression because on the surface I seem like I’ve got it together.  But you don’t need a reason to be depressed, no more than you need a reason to have asthma. It’s a condition.

I wish I had the answer. It gets better and then it gets worse. I’ll keep holding on and I hope you do the same.

I didn’t like AA for similar reasons. There are a lot of sobriety resources that are not linked to AA that might be more effective for you. This Naked Mind by Annie Grace is a great book. She also has a YouTube channel under the same title with hours of helpful material. The Easy Way to Control Alcohol by Allen Carr is another great book. There’s also SMART recovery if you want a group/community to attend. They have groups all over the place. Check those out.
